abstract: Through a series of randomized controlled trials with 1,222 participants, Liu and Christian provide causal evidence that AI assistance reduces human persistence and impairs unassisted performance. Across tasks including mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension, participants who received AI assistance performed significantly worse when later working without AI and were more likely to give up on challenging problems. These effects emerged after only approximately 10 minutes of AI interaction. The authors argue that current AI systems are fundamentally short-sighted collaborators — optimized for providing instant and complete responses without scaffolding learning or prioritizing the user's long-term growth. Because persistence is foundational to skill acquisition and among the strongest predictors of long-term learning, the findings raise concerns about AI's impact on human capital development. The results suggest that AI model development should prioritize scaffolding long-term competence alongside immediate task completion.
keyFindings: AI assistance causes reduced persistence and impaired independent performance, demonstrated through randomized controlled trials with 1,222 participants across mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension tasks.
Effects emerge after only approximately 10 minutes of AI interaction, suggesting even brief AI use can alter problem-solving behavior and willingness to persevere through challenges.
Although AI assistance improves short-term task performance, participants subsequently perform significantly worse without AI and are more likely to give up on novel problems.
Current AI systems function as short-sighted collaborators optimized for instant answers, denying users the experience of working through challenges that builds long-term competence.
Persistence — one of the strongest predictors of long-term learning and skill acquisition — is reduced because AI conditions users to expect immediate answers.
methodology: Series of randomized controlled trials (N = 1,222) examining human-AI interactions across multiple task types including mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension. Participants were randomly assigned to AI-assisted or unassisted conditions, then tested on subsequent independent tasks to measure persistence and unaided performance. The experimental design provides causal identification of AI's effects on human behavior.
qualifiers: arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. The experimental tasks (math reasoning, reading comprehension) may not generalize to all work contexts. The 10-minute interaction window is brief — longer-term or repeated AI use could produce different (possibly stronger) effects. The study measures laboratory behavior, and real-world persistence dynamics may differ. The findings focus on current AI systems' default behavior and may not apply to AI tools specifically designed to scaffold learning.
